# Windowed analyses

A genome-scale alignment decoded in one job is a single long-running task that cannot
use more than one node and has to start over if it fails. Setting `window_size` turns
the decoding into one job per window, which a cluster can run in parallel:

```yaml
analyses:
  - name: primates
    maf: data/alignment.maf
    config: config/itrails_config.yaml
    window_size: 2000000
    species: [hg38, panTro5, gorGor5, ponAbe2]
```

## Why this is lossless

iTRAILS treats every MAF block as an independent sequence: the HMM runs along a
block and starts afresh at the next one, with no transition across the boundary.
Splitting the alignment *at block boundaries* therefore cannot change any result — a
window is just a subset of blocks handed to the same model.

What windowing does not do is subdivide a block. A block that straddles a boundary
belongs to the window its start position falls in, so windows are approximate at
block granularity. With 1 Mb blocks and 2 Mb windows, a "2 Mb" window holds two or
three blocks.

## Which coordinates define a window

Blocks are binned by the start coordinate of one species' line in each block: the
`reference` species if you set one, otherwise the first sequence line of the block,
which is the MAF convention for the reference genome. Windows are numbered `w0000`,
`w0001`, … in file order, restarting the numbering at neither chromosome nor
contig — the label is a running index, and the chromosome is recorded alongside it in
the manifests.

::: { .callout-note }

## Set `species` to your `species_list`

iTRAILS silently skips alignment blocks that are missing one of the four species. If
the splitter kept those blocks, the block indices iTRAILS reports would no longer
line up with the manifest, and the genome coordinates in the concatenated output
would be wrong. Setting `species` makes the splitter drop exactly the same blocks.
The concatenation step checks for the mismatch and fails with an explanation rather
than writing misplaced coordinates.

For VCF input this is automatic: `species` defaults to `samples`.

:::

## Fitting once or per window

`fit: genome` (the default) runs one `itrails-optimize` on the whole alignment and
decodes every window with that model. Parameters like ancestral population size and
split time are properties of the species history rather than of a particular
megabase, so this is the usual setup, and it is also the cheap one — the expensive
step runs once.

`fit: window` runs a separate optimization for each window, and each window is then
decoded with its own model. This is what you want if the *variation* of the estimates
along the genome is the object of study, for instance to look for regions with
unusual levels of incomplete lineage sorting.

::: { .callout-warning }

`fit: window` multiplies the expensive step by the number of windows: a mammalian
genome at 2 Mb is on the order of 1,500 optimization jobs. Estimates from a single
2 Mb window are also noisy, since the parameters are being fit to far less data than
the model was designed for. Treat the result as a scan, not as 1,500 independent
answers.

:::

## What the workflow creates

A windowed analysis with two windows produces these targets:

```txt
itrails_split_{name}              alignment  →  split/w0000.maf, w0001.maf, manifests
itrails_optimize_{name}           alignment  →  optimize/{name}.best_model.yaml
itrails_viterbi_{name}_w0000      window     →  viterbi/w0000.viterbi.csv
itrails_viterbi_{name}_w0001      window     →  viterbi/w0001.viterbi.csv
itrails_posterior_{name}_w0000    window     →  posterior/w0000.posterior.csv
itrails_posterior_{name}_w0001    window     →  posterior/w0001.posterior.csv
itrails_concat_viterbi_{name}     windows    →  concat/{name}.viterbi.csv
itrails_concat_posterior_{name}   windows    →  concat/{name}.posterior.csv
```

With `fit: window` the single optimize target is replaced by one per window, named
`itrails_optimize_{name}_w0000` and writing `optimize/w0000.best_model.yaml`.

The concatenation step stacks the per-window CSVs back into one file per decode kind
and prefixes every row with the columns needed to place it on the genome. See
[Output files](outputs.qmd).

## When windows are computed

Window boundaries are worked out **when the workflow is defined**, not when it runs,
because GWF needs to know the file names of every target up front. How that is done
depends on the input:

| Input | Source of the window boundaries |
|:---|:---|
| `maf` | a scan of the alignment, cached by file size and modification time |
| `vcf` with `fasta` | contig lengths from the FASTA index `{fasta}.fai` |
| `vcf` without `fasta` | contig lengths from the `##contig` header lines |

For a MAF this means the alignment has to exist before `gwf run` can build the
workflow; if an upstream target produces it, run that part first. The scan result is
cached in `split/.window_index.json` so that repeated `gwf status` calls do not
re-read a large alignment.

VCF analyses are exempt from that constraint, because the converter tiles every
contig with blocks of a known size — the windows follow from the contig lengths
alone. What they need instead is a FASTA index, created once with
`samtools faidx <reference>.fa`, or `length=` on every `##contig` line.

## Practical notes

- The per-window decode options apply to each window job. Ask for the memory one
  window needs, not the whole genome.
- The concatenated posterior file has one row per alignment position and one column
  per hidden state. For a mammalian genome with 27 states that is very large; the
  per-window files are often the more practical thing to read.
- Windows are independent, so a failed window can be rerun on its own with
  `gwf run itrails_viterbi_{name}_w0042`.
